Real US states (watch out for fakes).New Jersey: Named after the Channel Island of Jersey, it has more diners than any other state and is the most densely populated.
Real US states (watch out for fakes).West Virginia: It is the only state created by seceding from a Confederate state, splitting from Virginia during the Civil War in 1863.
Real US states (watch out for fakes).Rhode Island: Its official name is State of Rhode Island and Providence Plantations, the longest of any state, although voters dropped the second part in 2020.
Real US states (watch out for fakes).North Dakota: Its small population, around 780,000, and bitter winters make it one of the least visited states.
Real US states (watch out for fakes).South Carolina: The first shots of the Civil War were fired at Fort Sumter in Charleston Harbor, in 1861.
Real US states (watch out for fakes).Washington: The only state named for a president, it is a different place from Washington, D.C., which is not a state.
Real US states (watch out for fakes).Virginia: The oldest English colony that lasted, founded at Jamestown in 1607, and the birthplace of eight US presidents.
Real US states (watch out for fakes).Delaware: The first state, ratifying the Constitution on December 7, 1787, and it has just three counties.
Real US states (watch out for fakes).Georgia: Named after Britain's King George II, it produces more peanuts than any other state, and has a country of the same name in the Caucasus.
Real US states (watch out for fakes).Indiana: The Hoosier State's name roughly means land of the Indians, and it borders Lake Michigan to the northwest.
Real US states (watch out for fakes).New Mexico: It became a state in 1912, and it was named by Spanish explorers long before Mexico was a country of that name.
Real US states (watch out for fakes).East Virginia: Trap: invented. There is a Virginia and a West Virginia, but no East Virginia on the map.
Real US states (watch out for fakes).West Dakota: Trap: invented. The Dakota Territory split into North and South, and no state called West Dakota exists.
Real US states (watch out for fakes).North Virginia: Trap: invented. Northern Virginia is a region, not a state, and includes Arlington and Alexandria.
Real US states (watch out for fakes).New Vermont: Trap: invented. Vermont's name is from the French for green mountain, and 'new' is not part of it.
Real US states (watch out for fakes).South Montana: Trap: invented. Montana is a single state, and has no southern counterpart.
Real US states (watch out for fakes).New Ohio: Trap: invented. Ohio never had a New version, though New Philadelphia and New Concord do exist as towns there.
Real US states (watch out for fakes).West Carolina: Trap: invented. The Carolinas split into North and South in 1712, and no west one existed.
Real US states (watch out for fakes).Lower Michigan: Trap: invented as a state, though the Lower Peninsula is the part of Michigan shaped like a mitten.
Real US states (watch out for fakes).Long Island: Trap: an island and not a state, and it is mostly part of New York and holds Brooklyn and Queens.
Real US states (watch out for fakes).New England: Trap: a region of six states, among them Maine and Vermont, but not itself a state.
Real US states (watch out for fakes).Dakota: Trap: a former territory that split into North Dakota and South Dakota in 1889, so it is not a state.
Real US states (watch out for fakes).Carolina: Trap: the colony was divided into North Carolina and South Carolina, so no single state by this name exists.

Fictional or legendary places.Narnia: C. S. Lewis's land, first visited through a wardrobe in 1950, is ruled by the lion Aslan.
Fictional or legendary places.Hogwarts: The school in the Harry Potter books has four houses, and its Scottish castle look was based on places like Alnwick Castle, used in the films.
Fictional or legendary places.Mordor: Tolkien's dark land has its name from Black Speech, and means black land, home of Mount Doom.
Fictional or legendary places.Atlantis: Plato described it as an island that sank in a day and a night, and it is likely a parable he invented.
Fictional or legendary places.Gotham City: Batman's city got its name from a nickname for New York, which is itself taken from an English village known for foolishness.
Fictional or legendary places.Neverland: J. M. Barrie's island first appeared in the 1904 play Peter Pan, and it is the home of the Lost Boys.
Fictional or legendary places.Wakanda: This hidden African nation first appeared in Marvel's Fantastic Four in 1966, and it is the home of Black Panther.
Fictional or legendary places.Westeros: The continent in George R. R. Martin's A Song of Ice and Fire holds the Seven Kingdoms and the Wall.
Fictional or legendary places.Bikini Bottom: SpongeBob's undersea town is named after Bikini Atoll, where the US tested nuclear bombs.
Fictional or legendary places.Lilliput: Jonathan Swift invented this land of tiny people in Gulliver's Travels in 1726, and the word now means tiny.
Fictional or legendary places.Shangri-La: James Hilton invented it in the 1933 novel Lost Horizon as a hidden Himalayan paradise, and the name now means any earthly paradise.
Fictional or legendary places.Middle-earth: Tolkien's world for The Hobbit and The Lord of the Rings; its name echoes an old English term for the world of humans.
Fictional or legendary places.Asgard: The home of the Norse gods, linked by the rainbow bridge Bifrost to Midgard, the world of humans.
Fictional or legendary places.Timbuktu: Trap: it is a real city in Mali, which was a famed center of Islamic learning and trade, even though its name means a faraway place.
Fictional or legendary places.Kathmandu: Trap: Nepal's real capital, nestled in a valley, is not a mythical place.
Fictional or legendary places.Ouagadougou: Trap: the real capital of Burkina Faso, with a name that sounds like a made-up word.
Fictional or legendary places.Zanzibar: Trap: an island of Tanzania with Stone Town, and the birthplace of Freddie Mercury.
Fictional or legendary places.Kalamazoo: Trap: a real city in Michigan, which sounds silly and is mentioned in a Glenn Miller song.
Fictional or legendary places.Walla Walla: Trap: a real city in Washington state, famous for its sweet onions, and the name means many waters.
Fictional or legendary places.Bora Bora: Trap: a real island in French Polynesia, known for its overwater bungalows.
Fictional or legendary places.Samarkand: Trap: a real Silk Road city in Uzbekistan that is among the oldest inhabited places in Central Asia.
Fictional or legendary places.Llandudno: Trap: a real Welsh seaside town, where Alice Liddell's family had a holiday home.
Fictional or legendary places.Casablanca: Trap: Morocco's biggest city is real, though the 1942 film was shot entirely in Hollywood.
Fictional or legendary places.Tuvalu: Trap: it sounds like a made-up place, but it is a real Pacific island country.

Man-made canals (not natural straits).Suez Canal: Opened in 1869, it links the Mediterranean to the Red Sea and spares ships the long voyage around Africa. In 2021 one stuck container ship blocked it for six days.
Man-made canals (not natural straits).Panama Canal: It lifts ships about 26 metres up to Gatun Lake through locks, then lowers them again. The Americas' two oceans are joined by a staircase of water.
Man-made canals (not natural straits).Welland Canal: This Canadian canal lets ships bypass Niagara Falls, climbing about 100 metres between Lake Erie and Lake Ontario through a series of locks.
Man-made canals (not natural straits).Erie Canal: Finished in 1825, it connected the Hudson River to Lake Erie and helped make New York City the nation's leading port.
Man-made canals (not natural straits).Kiel Canal: Cutting across northern Germany, it saves ships a trip around Denmark and is often cited as the world's busiest artificial seaway by ship traffic.
Man-made canals (not natural straits).Corinth Canal: Barely 6 kilometres long yet cut through solid rock with sheer walls, it slices the Peloponnese off from mainland Greece. Many modern ships are too wide for it.
Man-made canals (not natural straits).Caledonian Canal: Built partly to link Scotland's lochs, it joins coast to coast across the Highlands and passes through Loch Ness, so boaters share the water with the monster legend.
Man-made canals (not natural straits).Canal du Midi: Completed in 1681 in southern France, it linked the Atlantic to the Mediterranean and is a UNESCO World Heritage Site lined with plane trees.
Man-made canals (not natural straits).Göta Canal: Nicknamed Sweden's blue ribbon, this 19th-century canal crosses the country through lakes and locks and is now a popular holiday route for slow cruising.
Man-made canals (not natural straits).Rideau Canal: Running through Ottawa, it becomes a skating rink in winter, billed as the world's largest naturally frozen rink, stretching about 7.8 kilometres.
Man-made canals (not natural straits).Bosporus: A natural strait splitting Istanbul between Europe and Asia. Though only about 700 metres wide at its narrowest, it carries huge tanker traffic.
Man-made canals (not natural straits).Dardanelles: This natural strait, ancient Hellespont, links the Aegean to the Sea of Marmara. Legend says Leander swam across it nightly to meet his lover.
Man-made canals (not natural straits).Strait of Hormuz: A natural chokepoint between Iran and Oman, through which roughly a fifth of the world's oil passes. It is only about 39 kilometres wide at its narrowest.
Man-made canals (not natural straits).English Channel: A natural waterway between England and France, about 33 kilometres wide at the Dover Strait. The Channel Tunnel runs beneath it, but nobody dug the water itself.
Man-made canals (not natural straits).Strait of Magellan: Named for Ferdinand Magellan, who found this natural winding passage at South America's tip in 1520, long before the Panama Canal offered a shortcut.
Man-made canals (not natural straits).Bering Strait: A natural gap of roughly 85 kilometres separating Russia from Alaska. Ice-age hunters crossed here when lower seas exposed a land bridge.
Man-made canals (not natural straits).Strait of Malacca: A natural channel between Malaysia and Sumatra, one of the busiest shipping lanes on Earth, linking the Indian Ocean to the Pacific.
Man-made canals (not natural straits).Gulf of Aden: A natural body of water between Yemen and Somalia, famous in modern times for piracy and the naval patrols that guard its shipping.
Man-made canals (not natural straits).Bay of Biscay: A natural bay off France and Spain, notorious for rough seas and storms. It's also one of Europe's best places to spot whales and dolphins.
Man-made canals (not natural straits).Drake Passage: Between Cape Horn and Antarctica, this natural stretch has some of the roughest seas anywhere, known to polar travellers as the Drake Shake.
Man-made canals (not natural straits).Cook Strait: A natural channel separating New Zealand's North and South Islands. Wellington's ferries cross it, and its winds and currents are notoriously fierce.
Man-made canals (not natural straits).Hudson Bay: A vast inland sea in Canada, not a canal at all. It is so big and shallow that its freshwater input makes it far less salty than the oceans.
Man-made canals (not natural straits).Strait of Dover: The natural narrowest point of the English Channel, where on a clear day you can see France's white cliffs from England's.
Man-made canals (not natural straits).Solent: A natural strait between the Isle of Wight and mainland England, famed for sailing and for its unusual double high tide.

Vitamins.Vitamin A: Needed for vision, especially in dim light, it's found in carrots as beta-carotene, and too much of the animal form can be toxic.
Vitamins.Vitamin C: Sailors on long voyages got scurvy without it, and citrus fruit prevented the disease long before anyone knew why.
Vitamins.Vitamin D: Your skin makes it from sunlight, which is why it's called the sunshine vitamin, and it helps absorb calcium for bones.
Vitamins.Vitamin E: An antioxidant found in nuts and seeds, protecting cell membranes from damage, and wheat germ oil is among the richest sources.
Vitamins.Vitamin K: Its name comes from the German word Koagulation, because it helps blood clot, and gut bacteria make some of it.
Vitamins.Vitamin B12: Only found naturally in animal foods, so vegans need a supplement, and the body can store years' worth in the liver.
Vitamins.Thiamine: It was the first B vitamin discovered, and its lack caused beriberi in people eating polished white rice.
Vitamins.Riboflavin: Also called vitamin B2, it gives urine a bright yellow color when you take supplements.
Vitamins.Niacin: Also called vitamin B3, its deficiency causes pellagra, which was once common among people living on corn-based diets.
Vitamins.Folate: Its name comes from foliage, because it's found in leafy greens, and it helps prevent birth defects in early pregnancy.
Vitamins.Biotin: Also called vitamin B7, it supports hair and nails, but a deficiency is rare, though raw egg whites can block it.
Vitamins.Iron: A mineral, not a vitamin, which carries oxygen in blood, and women need more of it during menstruation.
Vitamins.Calcium: A mineral needed for bones and teeth, and about 99 percent of the body's supply is stored in the skeleton.
Vitamins.Zinc: A mineral, not a vitamin, which supports immunity and wound healing, and found in oysters in large amounts.
Vitamins.Magnesium: A mineral, not a vitamin, important for nerves and muscles, and found in nuts, seeds and leafy greens.
Vitamins.Potassium: A mineral that helps balance fluids and heart rhythm, and bananas are famous for it but not the richest source.
Vitamins.Omega-3: A fatty acid, not a vitamin, found in oily fish and flax, linked to heart and brain health.
Vitamins.Protein: It's a macronutrient, built from amino acids, not a vitamin, and your body can't store it as a reserve.
Vitamins.Fiber: Plant-derived roughage that is a carbohydrate, not a vitamin, and which your body can't digest.
Vitamins.Iodine: A mineral needed to make thyroid hormones, and it's added to table salt to prevent goiter.
Vitamins.Sodium: A mineral, not a vitamin, and the sodium in table salt, it's essential for nerves, but most people get too much.
Vitamins.Cholesterol: A fat-like substance, not a vitamin, which your liver makes itself, and it's needed for cell membranes and hormones.
Vitamins.Caffeine: A stimulant found in coffee, not a vitamin, and it's the world's most widely used psychoactive substance.
Vitamins.Glucose: The simple sugar that fuels your cells, especially the brain, which uses about a fifth of the body's energy; it's a sugar, not a vitamin.

True berries (botanically).Banana: Botanically a berry, with a leathery skin as the wall. The wild ancestors were full of hard seeds, and the seedless kind we eat is a human-bred oddity.
True berries (botanically).Grape: A classic true berry: soft flesh around seeds, all from a single ovary. Wine, raisins and juice all come from this one botanical berry.
True berries (botanically).Tomato: Botanically a berry, though a 1893 US Supreme Court ruling called it a vegetable for tariff purposes. Science and the law still disagree.
True berries (botanically).Blueberry: A true berry that grows from a flower with the ovary below the petals. The dusty bloom on its skin is a natural wax coating.
True berries (botanically).Kiwi fruit: Its fuzzy skin hides a true berry with tiny edible seeds. It was once called Chinese gooseberry before being rebranded after New Zealand's bird.
True berries (botanically).Eggplant: Related to the tomato and potato, and a true berry too. Some early European varieties were small, white and egg-shaped, hence the name.
True berries (botanically).Chili pepper: Each pod is a true berry, even the fiery ones. Birds don't feel capsaicin, so they spread the seeds while mammals get the burn.
True berries (botanically).Cranberry: A true berry that grows on low trailing vines. Cranberry fruits contain tiny air pockets, which is why they float and are harvested in flooded bogs.
True berries (botanically).Gooseberry: A true berry with translucent, veined skin. In the 1800s it was so beloved in Britain that gooseberry-growing contests were serious competitions.
True berries (botanically).Persimmon: Botanically a berry, even though it can be as large as a tomato. Unripe fruit of many types is intensely astringent, thanks to tannins.
True berries (botanically).Strawberry: Not a berry at all. The juicy red part is swollen flower base, and the true fruits are the tiny 'seeds' on its surface, each a separate achene.
True berries (botanically).Raspberry: Despite the name, it's an aggregate of tiny drupelets, each with its own seed. When picked, it pulls free of its core and leaves a hollow cup.
True berries (botanically).Blackberry: Another aggregate fruit made of many little drupelets, not a true berry. Each bump on it was a separate ovary of one flower.
True berries (botanically).Mulberry: A cluster of many tiny fruits fused together, so it's a multiple fruit, not a berry. Silkworms feed exclusively on the leaves of the white mulberry.
True berries (botanically).Cherry: A drupe, with a hard pit surrounding the seed, which rules out berry status. True berries have seeds embedded directly in soft flesh.
True berries (botanically).Peach: A drupe: its stony pit encloses the seed. Peaches and almonds are close relatives, which is why a peach pit smells faintly of almond.
True berries (botanically).Apple: A pome, in which the core is the true fruit and the flesh grows from the flower's base. Apples are in the rose family, alongside pears.
True berries (botanically).Pear: A pome like the apple, where most of the flesh develops from the flower tube rather than the ovary. Those gritty cells in pears are called stone cells.
True berries (botanically).Plum: A drupe with a single hard stone. Dried plums are prunes, and the fruit's powdery bloom is a natural wax coating.
True berries (botanically).Mango: A drupe, with a large flat stone in the middle. It's the national fruit of India and is related to cashews and poison ivy.
True berries (botanically).Olive: A drupe, though it sounds berry-like. Freshly picked olives are painfully bitter and must be cured before they're edible.
True berries (botanically).Boysenberry: A hybrid of raspberry, blackberry and loganberry, so it's an aggregate fruit. It was popularized by Walter Knott at Knott's Berry Farm in California.
True berries (botanically).Pineapple: A multiple fruit made from dozens of fused flowers, each one of the diamond-shaped segments. It takes about two years to grow a single fruit.
True berries (botanically).Fig: Technically an inverted flower, with the tiny flowers inside a hollow pod, so the fruit is a syconium. Special wasps pollinate many species.

Compounds made of exactly two elements.Water: Just hydrogen and oxygen, and it is the only common substance that occurs naturally as solid, liquid and gas at Earth's surface.
Compounds made of exactly two elements.Carbon dioxide: Carbon plus oxygen makes up about 0.04% of the air, and its solid form, dry ice, sits at about minus 78 degrees Celsius.
Compounds made of exactly two elements.Sodium chloride: Table salt pairs an explosive metal with a poisonous gas and makes something your body cannot live without.
Compounds made of exactly two elements.Methane: The main part of natural gas, CH4; livestock release it mostly by burping, not the other end.
Compounds made of exactly two elements.Ammonia: Just nitrogen and hydrogen, and making it from air for fertiliser helps grow food for roughly half of humanity.
Compounds made of exactly two elements.Hydrogen peroxide: It is water with one extra oxygen; the fizzing on a cut is an enzyme in your cells breaking it back into water and oxygen.
Compounds made of exactly two elements.Carbon monoxide: It binds to haemoglobin more than 200 times as tightly as oxygen does, which is why this odourless gas is so dangerous.
Compounds made of exactly two elements.Hydrogen chloride: A gas that turns into hydrochloric acid in water, and your stomach makes its own to digest food.
Compounds made of exactly two elements.Propane: Only carbon and hydrogen, stored as a liquid under pressure; a smelly additive is added so leaks are noticed.
Compounds made of exactly two elements.Quartz: Silicon dioxide, and quartz crystals vibrate at a steady rate when electrified, which keeps most watches accurate.
Compounds made of exactly two elements.Nitrous oxide: Laughing gas, N2O, was used in dentistry from the 1840s and now also powers whipped-cream chargers.
Compounds made of exactly two elements.Sugar: Table sugar is C12H22O11, carbon, hydrogen and oxygen, so three elements, not two.
Compounds made of exactly two elements.Baking soda: NaHCO3 contains sodium, hydrogen, carbon and oxygen, so four elements.
Compounds made of exactly two elements.Ethanol: C2H6O has carbon, hydrogen and oxygen, so three; it is the alcohol in drinks.
Compounds made of exactly two elements.Acetic acid: C2H4O2 has three elements, and vinegar is typically about 5% of it in water.
Compounds made of exactly two elements.Chalk: Real chalk is calcium carbonate, three elements, though many modern classroom sticks are actually gypsum.
Compounds made of exactly two elements.Sulfuric acid: H2SO4 contains hydrogen, sulfur and oxygen, so three elements, and it is one of the most-produced industrial chemicals.
Compounds made of exactly two elements.Glucose: C6H12O6 has three elements, and your brain runs largely on it.
Compounds made of exactly two elements.Caffeine: Four elements: carbon, hydrogen, nitrogen and oxygen.
Compounds made of exactly two elements.Aspirin: C9H8O4, three elements; its roots lie in a compound from willow bark.
Compounds made of exactly two elements.Diamond: A trap: diamond is pure carbon, a single element, so it is not a compound at all, and it has the same atoms as pencil graphite.
Compounds made of exactly two elements.Ozone: O3 is only oxygen atoms, so ozone is a pure element in another form, not a compound.
Compounds made of exactly two elements.Gold: A single element, Au, so it cannot be a compound.
Compounds made of exactly two elements.Bleach: Household bleach is sodium hypochlorite, NaClO, three elements dissolved in water.

Pixar films.Toy Story: In 1995 it became the first fully computer-animated feature film, and it took Pixar about four years to make it.
Pixar films.Up: Its opening wordless montage of a couple's life together famously made audiences cry, and it was a Best Picture nominee.
Pixar films.Cars: The road trip in Cars was inspired by Route 66, and the town of Radiator Springs was modeled on real towns along it.
Pixar films.Coco: This 2017 film is built around Día de los Muertos, and its song 'Remember Me' won an Oscar. Mexican consultants helped shape it.
Pixar films.Ratatouille: A rat chef in Paris, and the dish that wins over the critic is a humble peasant stew, not a fancy meal.
Pixar films.WALL-E: The first act has almost no dialogue, and sound designer Ben Burtt made WALL-E's voice. He also created R2-D2's beeps.
Pixar films.Inside Out: Director Pete Docter based it on his daughter's growing up, and consulted psychologists on how emotions work.
Pixar films.Brave: Merida is Pixar's first female lead, and the film is set in the Scottish Highlands. It won the Oscar for animated feature.
The film's Sulley model had over 2 million hairs, a technical feat in 2001.
Pixar films.Finding Nemo: After release, demand for clownfish rose, and conservationists worried. Nemo and Marlin's anemone home is real.
Pixar films.The Incredibles: Brad Bird wrote the superhero family story, and it was Pixar's first film with all human characters.
Pixar films.Luca: Luca takes place on the Italian Riviera, with sea monsters who look human on land. Its look was inspired by Hayao Miyazaki.
Pixar films.Soul: Soul was released straight to Disney+ in 2020 and won Best Animated Feature. Jazz musician Jon Batiste composed the jazz music.
Pixar films.Shrek: DreamWorks, not Pixar, made Shrek in 2001. It won the first Oscar for Best Animated Feature.
Pixar films.Frozen: Frozen is from Disney Animation, not Pixar. Its song 'Let It Go' won an Oscar.
Pixar films.Moana: Disney Animation made Moana, with songs by Lin-Manuel Miranda. It's not Pixar.
Pixar films.Madagascar: DreamWorks made Madagascar, with penguins that got their own spinoff. It's not Pixar.
Pixar films.Kung Fu Panda: DreamWorks Animation makes Kung Fu Panda, starring Jack Black as Po. Not Pixar.
Pixar films.Despicable Me: Illumination, not Pixar, made the film that launched the Minions. The yellow henchmen later got their own films.
Pixar films.Tangled: Tangled came from Disney Animation, and was among the most expensive animated films ever made. It's not Pixar.
Pixar films.Zootopia: Zootopia is from Disney Animation. Its animals were designed with different scales so every species fits.
Pixar films.Encanto: Encanto is a Disney Animation film, famous for the hit 'We Don't Talk About Bruno'. Not Pixar.
Pixar films.Ice Age: Blue Sky Studios made Ice Age, whose acorn-chasing squirrel Scrat stole scenes. Not Pixar.
Pixar films.Megamind: DreamWorks Animation made Megamind, a villain-turned-hero story. Not Pixar.

Musical terms about loudness.Forte: Written f, it means loud, from the Italian for strong, and one of the most common dynamic markings of all.
Musical terms about loudness.Piano: Soft. The instrument got its name from being able to play both soft and loud, unlike the harpsichord, which can't change volume by touch.
Musical terms about loudness.Fortissimo: Written ff, very loud. Composers sometimes pile on more letters, as in fff, for truly thundering moments.
Musical terms about loudness.Pianissimo: Written pp, very soft. Tchaikovsky once marked a bassoon passage pppppp in his Pathétique Symphony.
Musical terms about loudness.Mezzo forte: Written mf, it's moderately loud, and is the most common middle dynamic, the default level of a lot of music.
Musical terms about loudness.Mezzo piano: Written mp, moderately soft, only a touch quieter than mezzo forte, and mezzo means half in Italian.
Musical terms about loudness.Crescendo: Gradually getting louder. Ravel's Boléro is essentially one long crescendo lasting around a quarter of an hour.
Musical terms about loudness.Diminuendo: Gradually getting softer, and the same idea as decrescendo. It is often shown by a long closing angle bracket.
Musical terms about loudness.Sforzando: Written sfz, a sudden forceful accent on one note. The word comes from the Italian for forcing.
Musical terms about loudness.Decrescendo: Gradually getting softer, the same thing as diminuendo, with decrescendo more common in band and choir music.
Musical terms about loudness.Allegro: A tempo marking meaning fast and lively. It describes how quickly the music moves, not how loudly it's played.
Musical terms about loudness.Adagio: A slow tempo marking, from Italian for at ease. It says how fast, not how loud, to play.
Musical terms about loudness.Staccato: Short and detached notes, an articulation rather than a volume, shown with a dot above or below the note.
Musical terms about loudness.Legato: Smooth and connected, again about how notes join and not how loud, and it's marked with a curved slur.
Musical terms about loudness.Presto: A very fast tempo, not a volume. It's one of the most common speed markings in classical music.
Musical terms about loudness.Andante: A walking-pace tempo, so about speed, not loudness. The word comes from the Italian for walking.
Musical terms about loudness.Fermata: A pause symbol, sometimes called the bird's eye, that holds a note longer than written, with no effect on loudness.
Musical terms about loudness.Coda: The final section of a piece, from the Italian for tail. It's a structural term, not a dynamic.
Musical terms about loudness.Tremolo: Rapid repetition of a note or alternation of two. It's a technique, and can sound shaky but isn't a loudness marking.
Musical terms about loudness.Pizzicato: Plucked strings, a technique rather than a loudness marking, and it can be played softly or loudly.
Musical terms about loudness.Glissando: A slide between notes, as in the clarinet's opening wail in Rhapsody in Blue, and not a dynamic.
Musical terms about loudness.Arpeggio: The notes of a chord played one after another, from the Italian for harp-like. Nothing to do with volume.
Musical terms about loudness.Largo: A very slow tempo, from the Italian for broad. It's about speed, not about how loud.
Musical terms about loudness.Ritardando: Gradually slowing down, from the Italian for delaying, so a tempo change and not a loudness marking.

Andrew Lloyd Webber musicals.Cats: Based on T. S. Eliot's poems, it ran in London for 21 years from 1981, and its song Memory became a standard.
Andrew Lloyd Webber musicals.Evita: Tells the story of Eva Peron. Don't Cry for Me Argentina was first released on a 1976 concept album, before the stage show opened in 1978.
Andrew Lloyd Webber musicals.Phantom of the Opera: Opened in London in 1986 and became Broadway's longest-running show, finally closing in 2023 after 35 years.
Andrew Lloyd Webber musicals.Sunset Boulevard: Adapted from Billy Wilder's 1950 film about a faded silent-film star. Glenn Close won a Tony as Norma Desmond.
Andrew Lloyd Webber musicals.Starlight Express: The performers race each other on roller skates, and a German production in Bochum has run since 1988.
Andrew Lloyd Webber musicals.School of Rock: Based on the 2003 Jack Black film, with kid cast members playing their instruments live on stage.
Andrew Lloyd Webber musicals.Aspects of Love: This 1989 musical gave the world Love Changes Everything, a big UK hit for Michael Ball.
Andrew Lloyd Webber musicals.Love Never Dies: A 2010 sequel to Phantom, set a decade later in Coney Island.
Andrew Lloyd Webber musicals.Tell Me on a Sunday: A one-woman song cycle from 1979 that later became the first half of the show Song and Dance.
Andrew Lloyd Webber musicals.Les Misérables: Its music is by Claude-Michel Schonberg, not Lloyd Webber. Based on Victor Hugo's novel, it has played in London since 1985.
Andrew Lloyd Webber musicals.Miss Saigon: Made by the Les Mis team, not Lloyd Webber. It retells Madame Butterfly against the Vietnam War.
Andrew Lloyd Webber musicals.Wicked: Stephen Schwartz wrote this Wizard of Oz prequel, which opened on Broadway in 2003.
Andrew Lloyd Webber musicals.Hamilton: Lin-Manuel Miranda wrote the book, music and lyrics, and the show won the 2016 Pulitzer Prize for Drama.
Andrew Lloyd Webber musicals.Chicago: Written by Kander and Ebb, and its 1996 Broadway revival is among the longest-running shows ever.
Andrew Lloyd Webber musicals.Oklahoma!: Rodgers and Hammerstein's first collaboration, from 1943. Not by Lloyd Webber.
Andrew Lloyd Webber musicals.The Lion King: Elton John wrote its songs, but the lyricist was Tim Rice, who also wrote the words for Lloyd Webber's Evita.
Andrew Lloyd Webber musicals.Mamma Mia!: Benny and Bjorn of ABBA wrote the songs, so no Lloyd Webber here, despite being a huge West End hit.
Andrew Lloyd Webber musicals.Rent: Jonathan Larson died suddenly the night before its first off-Broadway preview in 1996, and never saw its success.
Andrew Lloyd Webber musicals.Grease: A 1971 Chicago creation by Jim Jacobs and Warren Casey. Not by Lloyd Webber.
Andrew Lloyd Webber musicals.Hairspray: Marc Shaiman wrote the songs, and the story comes from John Waters's 1988 film.
Andrew Lloyd Webber musicals.Annie: Charles Strouse wrote Tomorrow for this show based on the Little Orphan Annie comic strip.
Andrew Lloyd Webber musicals.Matilda: Tim Minchin wrote the songs for this Roald Dahl adaptation, which began at the Royal Shakespeare Company.
Andrew Lloyd Webber musicals.West Side Story: Bernstein and Sondheim's 1957 show moves Romeo and Juliet to New York. Not by Lloyd Webber.
Andrew Lloyd Webber musicals.The Sound of Music: Rodgers and Hammerstein's final collaboration opened in 1959, set in Austria.

Prince songs.1999: 1999 imagined partying while the world ended, and it became a surprise hit again as the real year arrived.
Prince songs.Purple Rain: Purple Rain is the 1984 title track, from the film of the same name, and it ends the album as a huge guitar ballad.
Prince songs.When Doves Cry: When Doves Cry hit number one in 1984 with no bass line at all, a daring choice for a pop hit.
Prince songs.Kiss: Kiss, from 1986, was built on a sparse funk groove, which Prince reworked from a demo he'd given to another group.
Prince songs.Little Red Corvette: Little Red Corvette was his first US top-10 hit, from 1983, with an extended car metaphor.
Prince songs.Raspberry Beret: Raspberry Beret is a bright, string-flecked 1985 single from Around the World in a Day.
Prince songs.Let's Go Crazy: Let's Go Crazy opens the Purple Rain album with an organ sermon and a ripping guitar solo.
Prince songs.Cream: Cream, from 1991, was a US number one, and one of his sleekest funk hits.
Prince songs.Sign o' the Times: Sign o' the Times is the 1987 title track of a double album, built on sparse drum machine and social commentary.
Prince songs.Diamonds and Pearls: Diamonds and Pearls is the 1991 title track, and the album spawned several of his later hits.
Prince songs.U Got the Look: U Got the Look is a 1987 duet with Sheena Easton, from Sign o' the Times.
Prince songs.Billie Jean: Billie Jean is Michael Jackson's 1983 classic, and not Prince's, despite their friendly rivalry.
Prince songs.Like a Virgin: Like a Virgin is Madonna's, from 1984, and written by Billy Steinberg and Tom Kelly.
Prince songs.Super Freak: Super Freak is Rick James's, from 1981, whose riff MC Hammer sampled for U Can't Touch This.
Prince songs.Let's Dance: Let's Dance is David Bowie's 1983 hit, produced by Nile Rodgers, not Prince.
Prince songs.Purple Haze: Purple Haze is Jimi Hendrix's, and despite the color, has nothing to do with Prince's purple.
Prince songs.Red Red Wine: Red Red Wine is UB40's, a reggae version of a song by Neil Diamond.
Prince songs.Thriller: Thriller is Michael Jackson's, from 1982, and the album became the biggest seller of all time.
Prince songs.Rapper's Delight: Rapper's Delight is the Sugarhill Gang's 1979 hit, among the first rap songs to reach the charts.
Prince songs.Celebration: Celebration is Kool & the Gang's 1980 hit, played at countless parties and victories.
Prince songs.Superstition: Superstition is Stevie Wonder's, from 1972, built on a funky clavinet riff.
Prince songs.I Feel Love: I Feel Love is Donna Summer's 1977 hit, produced by Giorgio Moroder and built entirely on synthesizers.
Prince songs.Material Girl: Material Girl is Madonna's 1984 hit, and it gave her one of her lasting nicknames.
Prince songs.Le Freak: Le Freak is Chic's 1978 hit, written after the group was turned away from Studio 54.

Darts terms.180: The maximum with three darts, three treble 20s, is announced with a long drawn-out shout.
Darts terms.Bullseye: Hitting the center of the board scores 50, which makes it the nickname for the inner ring.
Darts terms.Oche: The throwing line is pronounced 'ockey' and sits 7 feet 9.25 inches (2.37 m) from the board.
Darts terms.Treble: The narrow inner ring triples the number, so 20 treble is worth 60, the highest single-dart score.
Darts terms.Double: The thin outer ring doubles the score, and most games require finishing on one.
Darts terms.Checkout: The final dart that takes a player to exactly zero, with 170 as the largest possible finish.
Darts terms.Flights: These plastic or nylon fins at the back of the dart help it fly straight, like a feather on an arrow.
Darts terms.Barrel: Usually made of tungsten, it's the weighted part you grip, typically about 18 to 30 grams.
Darts terms.Bust: Going below zero, or leaving yourself on one, makes your turn count for nothing.
Darts terms.Shaft: The shaft is the stem that holds the flight, and it can be made of aluminum, nylon, or carbon.
Darts terms.Outer bull: The green ring around the bullseye scores 25 points, half the center's worth.
Darts terms.Nine-darter: A perfect leg in 501 in only nine darts, which is rare even for the pros.
Darts terms.Strike: In bowling, this means knocking down all ten pins with the first ball.
Darts terms.Spare: In bowling, a spare means knocking all the pins down with two rolls, using both balls.
Darts terms.Birdie: In golf, it means one under par, and has no place in darts.
Darts terms.Love: In tennis it means zero, and the word may come from the French l'oeuf, an egg.
Darts terms.Wicket: A cricket wicket is a target made of stumps and bails, and has no place on a dartboard.
Darts terms.Puck: The puck is an ice hockey disc, flat and hard, and darts have no such disc.
Darts terms.Cue: A cue is a pool or snooker stick, and there's no relation to the dart's barrel.
Darts terms.Ace: In tennis it's a serve that the opponent cannot touch, and in golf a hole in one, but not in darts.
Darts terms.Scrum: A rugby scrum is a formation where two packs of players push against each other, nothing like darts.
Darts terms.Bogey: Golfers say bogey for one over par, but in darts a 'bogey number' is a score that can't be finished in three darts.
Darts terms.Slam dunk: A slam dunk is a basketball shot thrown down through the hoop from above, and not a dart term.
Darts terms.Touchdown: A touchdown is a six-point scoring play in American football, not a dart term.

Things you'd find at a bowling alley.Pins: Ten pins are set in a triangle, and a regulation pin weighs about 3 pounds.
Things you'd find at a bowling alley.Lanes: A regulation lane is 60 feet from foul line to head pin and about 41 inches wide.
Things you'd find at a bowling alley.Bowling balls: House balls range from about 6 to 16 pounds, and the finger holes are drilled to fit your hand.
Things you'd find at a bowling alley.Rental shoes: Bowling shoes have a sliding sole on one foot so you can glide at release, which is why you must wear them.
Things you'd find at a bowling alley.Gutters: The gutters are channels on both sides of the lane where balls that go wide get lost.
Things you'd find at a bowling alley.Ball return: The return carries your ball back underground, which saves a walk and keeps the game flowing.
Things you'd find at a bowling alley.Scoreboard: Modern scoreboards calculate strikes and spares automatically, so nobody needs to keep a score.
Things you'd find at a bowling alley.Foul line: A sensor at the foul line detects when your foot crosses it, and in that case you score zero for the roll.
Things you'd find at a bowling alley.Pinsetter: Automatic pinsetters, first widely used in the 1950s, replaced the teenage pinboys who set pins by hand.
Things you'd find at a bowling alley.Bumpers: Bumpers, the padded rails that block the gutters, let kids roll a ball down the lane without scoring zero.
Things you'd find at a bowling alley.Approach: The approach is the raised area behind the foul line where you take your steps, usually about 15 feet long.
Things you'd find at a bowling alley.Shuttlecock: A shuttlecock is badminton's feathered projectile, and the fastest smash has been clocked at well over 400 kilometres an hour.
Things you'd find at a bowling alley.Puck: A puck is ice hockey's vulcanized rubber disc, one inch thick and three inches across, and it belongs on a rink, not a lane.
Things you'd find at a bowling alley.Tee: A tee holds a golf ball up for the first stroke of a hole, and its use is only allowed on the teeing ground.
Things you'd find at a bowling alley.Wicket: A wicket is cricket's target, three stumps topped with two bails, and the bowler tries to hit it to dismiss the batter.
Things you'd find at a bowling alley.Goalposts: Goalposts mark the target in soccer and rugby, and in American football they are a tall yellow fork behind the end zone.
Things you'd find at a bowling alley.Hoop: A basketball hoop is exactly 10 feet above the floor and 18 inches wide, and no bowling alley has one.
Things you'd find at a bowling alley.Zamboni: A Zamboni is the machine that resurfaces ice, invented by Frank Zamboni in 1949, and you would find it at a hockey rink.
Things you'd find at a bowling alley.Diving board: A diving board belongs at a swimming pool, and Olympic ones are three metres high, while platforms go as high as ten.
Things you'd find at a bowling alley.Saddle: A saddle sits on a horse's back, and it's not found in a bowling alley, but in stables and riding arenas.
Things you'd find at a bowling alley.Racket: A racket belongs to tennis, squash and badminton, and the strings are tightened to precise tension for control.
Things you'd find at a bowling alley.Pommel horse: The pommel horse is a gymnastics apparatus with two handles, on which gymnasts swing their legs in circles, and has no place here.
Things you'd find at a bowling alley.Halfpipe: A halfpipe is a U-shaped ramp for snowboarders and skateboarders, and Olympic snowboard halfpipes are about 22 feet deep.
Things you'd find at a bowling alley.Starting blocks: Starting blocks brace a sprinter's feet in track races, and they have been used since the 1930s to help with fast starts.

Sports organizations.FIFA: The governing body of world football, founded in Paris in 1904. It runs the men's and women's World Cups, which draw huge global TV audiences.
Sports organizations.IOC: The International Olympic Committee, based in Lausanne, Switzerland. It was founded in 1894 by Pierre de Coubertin, who revived the Games.
Sports organizations.UEFA: Europe's football body, which organizes the Champions League and the European Championship. It was founded in 1954 and is based in Nyon, Switzerland.
Sports organizations.FIBA: The international basketball federation, founded in 1932. It runs the Basketball World Cup and sets rules that differ slightly from the NBA's.
Sports organizations.World Rugby: The sport's global governing body, once known as the International Rugby Board. It is based in Dublin and oversees the Rugby World Cup.
Sports organizations.ITF: The International Tennis Federation, home of the Davis Cup and the Billie Jean King Cup. It also sets the rules of tennis, from ball size to court dimensions.
Sports organizations.FIDE: The World Chess Federation, founded in Paris in 1924. Its name comes from French, and it awards titles such as grandmaster and sets Elo ratings.
Sports organizations.FIA: The federation behind Formula 1, rallying and much more motorsport. Founded in 1904, it also looks after road safety and car clubs worldwide.
Sports organizations.UCI: The cycling union, based in Aigle, Switzerland. It governs the Tour de France calendar, sets rules on bikes, and enforces the hour record.
Sports organizations.WADA: The World Anti-Doping Agency, created in 1999 after a scandal at the Tour de France. It publishes the global list of banned substances every year.
Sports organizations.NCAA: The US body for college sports, founded in 1906 after deaths in football pushed President Roosevelt to demand safer rules.
Sports organizations.World Athletics: Track and field's global body, once the IAAF. Founded in 1912, it keeps world records and rules that cover everything from sprints to the marathon.
Sports organizations.NASA: America's space agency, formed in 1958. It is a government body for exploration, so it manages no sporting competitions despite its sporty competitiveness.
Sports organizations.NATO: A military alliance founded in 1949 with 12 members. It works on collective defense, so it's no sports body, though its logo has appeared on many posters.
Sports organizations.UNESCO: A UN agency for education, science and culture. It names World Heritage Sites, but sport falls outside its core role.
Sports organizations.WHO: The World Health Organization, a UN agency founded in 1948. It declared smallpox eradicated in 1980, yet sport is not its remit.
Sports organizations.IMF: The International Monetary Fund, formed in 1944, lends to countries in financial trouble. It tracks economies rather than athletes.
Sports organizations.OPEC: A group of oil-producing nations founded in 1960. Its decisions move fuel prices, but not game results.
Sports organizations.FBI: The Federal Bureau of Investigation, the US domestic law-enforcement agency, created in 1908. It has investigated sports corruption, such as FIFA bribery.
Sports organizations.CIA: The US foreign-intelligence agency, created in 1947. Despite its name, it has never overseen sports.
Sports organizations.UNICEF: The UN children's agency, formed in 1946. It partners with sports clubs, such as FC Barcelona, as a sponsor, but it is no governing body.
Sports organizations.Interpol: A global police cooperation network based in Lyon, France. It helps fight match-fixing but doesn't regulate any sport.
Sports organizations.NHS: The UK's National Health Service, launched in 1948. It treats sports injuries, yet it is a healthcare provider and not a governing body.
Sports organizations.BBC: The British Broadcasting Corporation, founded in 1922. It broadcasts huge sporting events, but it doesn't organize them.

Things usually made of cotton.T-shirt: The T-shirt began as a US Navy undergarment around 1913, and its T shape gave the name.
Things usually made of cotton.Jeans: Denim is a sturdy cotton twill, and its indigo dye fades because it coats the surface of the yarn rather than soaking in.
Things usually made of cotton.Bath towel: Cotton towels absorb well thanks to looped fibers, and long-staple Egyptian cotton makes them especially soft.
Things usually made of cotton.Cotton swab: The Q-tip was invented in the 1920s by Leo Gerstenzang after he saw his wife wrapping cotton around a toothpick.
Things usually made of cotton.Bedsheets: Thread count measures threads per square inch, but a higher number doesn't always mean better sheets.
Things usually made of cotton.Socks: Cotton socks soak up moisture and dry slowly, which is why hikers often prefer wool.
Things usually made of cotton.Cotton ball: Cotton fibers are almost pure cellulose, which is why a cotton ball soaks up so much liquid.
Things usually made of cotton.Tea towel: Linen was traditional, but cotton tea towels are popular since they wipe glassware without leaving lint.
Things usually made of cotton.Pillowcase: A cotton pillowcase is breathable, though silk or satin can be gentler on hair.
Things usually made of cotton.Bandana: The word comes from a Hindi term for tie-dye, and the classic paisley bandana was once a worker's staple.
Things usually made of cotton.Tote bag: Canvas totes are mostly cotton, and you'd need to use one many times to offset its larger footprint compared with a plastic bag.
Things usually made of cotton.Wool sweater: Wool comes from sheep, and its crimped fibers trap air to keep you warm even when damp.
Things usually made of cotton.Leather belt: Leather is animal hide tanned to make it durable, not a plant fiber like cotton.
Things usually made of cotton.Silk tie: Silk comes from silkworm cocoons, and a single cocoon can unwind into about a kilometer of thread.
Things usually made of cotton.Fleece jacket: Fleece is polyester, often made partly from recycled plastic bottles, so it's synthetic rather than cotton.
Things usually made of cotton.Rubber boots: Rubber boots are made from natural or synthetic rubber, waterproof and nothing like breathable cotton.
Things usually made of cotton.Plastic bag: Most plastic bags are polyethylene, a petroleum-based plastic that can take hundreds of years to break down.
Things usually made of cotton.Nylon tights: Nylon, introduced in 1939, was the first fully synthetic fiber, and its stockings sold out within hours.
Things usually made of cotton.Fur coat: Fur is animal hair and skin, warm but not plant-based like cotton.
Things usually made of cotton.Glass jar: A glass jar is melted sand, a hard, brittle material far from cotton's soft fibers.
Things usually made of cotton.Paper towel: Paper towels are wood pulp, not cotton, though early paper was made from cotton rags.
Things usually made of cotton.Sponge: Kitchen sponges are usually polyurethane foam or cellulose, not cotton, and the foam type can hold lots of bacteria.
Things usually made of cotton.Bubble wrap: Bubble wrap was invented in 1957 as textured wallpaper, and it's plastic rather than cotton.
Things usually made of cotton.Cork: Cork is bark from the cork oak tree, harvested without felling the tree, and it can regrow for decades.

Foods high in vitamin C.Orange: A medium orange gives most of a day's vitamin C, and its peel holds more of the fragrant oil than juice does.
Foods high in vitamin C.Lemon: British sailors were issued lemon and lime juice against scurvy, and the practice gave them the nickname 'limeys'.
Foods high in vitamin C.Kiwi: A kiwi can pack more vitamin C than an orange, and it's named after New Zealand's national bird.
Foods high in vitamin C.Strawberry: Strawberries are not true berries botanically, yet a cup delivers more than a day's vitamin C.
Foods high in vitamin C.Bell pepper: A red bell pepper has roughly twice the vitamin C of an orange, and it's the ripened version of green.
Foods high in vitamin C.Broccoli: Broccoli is rich in vitamin C, but long boiling washes much of it into the water.
Foods high in vitamin C.Grapefruit: Grapefruit is a good vitamin C source, but it can interfere with several medications, so doctors often warn about it.
Foods high in vitamin C.Guava: Guava has several times the vitamin C of an orange, making it one of the richest fruits in the world.
Foods high in vitamin C.Papaya: One papaya can supply over a day's worth of vitamin C, and its enzyme papain is used as a meat tenderizer.
Foods high in vitamin C.Pineapple: Pineapple has a good dose of vitamin C and an enzyme, bromelain, that breaks down protein, so it can tingle your tongue.
Foods high in vitamin C.Brussels sprouts: These tiny cabbages carry more vitamin C per serving than many fruits, and they're named after Brussels.
Foods high in vitamin C.Rice: A trap: rice is a starchy staple with almost no vitamin C, so sailors on rice-based diets still got scurvy.
Foods high in vitamin C.Bread: Bread offers carbs and some B vitamins but practically no vitamin C.
Foods high in vitamin C.Cheese: Cheese is rich in calcium and protein yet has essentially no vitamin C.
Foods high in vitamin C.Egg: Eggs are packed with protein and vitamin D, but they contain virtually no vitamin C.
Foods high in vitamin C.Chicken: Chicken is a protein source with little vitamin C, which is why meat-heavy diets need fruit and veg.
Foods high in vitamin C.Butter: Butter is almost all fat and carries vitamin A, but no vitamin C.
Foods high in vitamin C.Pasta: Pasta is a carbohydrate food with essentially no vitamin C unless the sauce brings tomatoes.
Foods high in vitamin C.Oatmeal: Oatmeal brings fiber and slow energy, but no vitamin C unless you top it with fruit.
Foods high in vitamin C.Milk: Milk supplies calcium and protein, but it's a surprisingly poor source of vitamin C, so babies on boiled milk were once at risk.
Foods high in vitamin C.Beef: Beef is a source of iron and zinc, and the iron in it is absorbed better when eaten with vitamin C foods.
Foods high in vitamin C.Peanut butter: Peanut butter is full of vitamin E and protein, but it has no meaningful vitamin C.
Foods high in vitamin C.Salmon: Salmon is rich in omega-3 fats and vitamin D, while vitamin C is almost absent.
Foods high in vitamin C.Tofu: Tofu is made from curdled soy milk and gives protein and calcium, but little vitamin C.

Exercises that mainly work your legs.Squat: A squat works the quads, glutes and hamstrings at once, and is often called the king of exercises because it recruits so many muscles.
Exercises that mainly work your legs.Lunge: Lunges train each leg separately, which exposes strength differences between your left and right sides.
Exercises that mainly work your legs.Leg press: A machine lets you push heavy weight with your legs while your back is supported, so people can load hundreds of kilograms.
Exercises that mainly work your legs.Calf raise: Calves are famously stubborn to grow, since they already work constantly while you walk.
Exercises that mainly work your legs.Step-up: Stepping onto a box with a single leg mimics climbing stairs, and builds balance as well as strength.
Exercises that mainly work your legs.Box jump: Box jumps train explosive power, and landing softly matters more than jumping higher.
Exercises that mainly work your legs.Wall sit: A wall sit holds the legs at a right angle against a wall, an isometric move where muscles work without moving.
Exercises that mainly work your legs.Leg curl: The leg curl isolates the hamstrings at the back of the thigh, which many people neglect.
Exercises that mainly work your legs.Pistol squat: A one-legged squat with the other leg out front, demanding strength, balance and flexibility in the ankle.
Exercises that mainly work your legs.Leg extension: This machine move isolates the quadriceps, the four-part muscle on the front of your thigh.
Exercises that mainly work your legs.Bicep curl: A trap: curls target the front of the upper arm, so while your legs stay still, they are not a leg move.
Exercises that mainly work your legs.Bench press: The bench press builds the chest, shoulders and triceps, and legs mostly just brace.
Exercises that mainly work your legs.Pull-up: Pull-ups work the back and arms, and the name for the lats comes from 'latissimus', Latin for widest.
Exercises that mainly work your legs.Push-up: Push-ups train chest, shoulders and triceps, and the core holds your body straight as a plank.
Exercises that mainly work your legs.Crunch: Crunches target the abdominal muscles and not the legs, and spot-reducing belly fat with them doesn't work.
Exercises that mainly work your legs.Tricep dip: Dips work the triceps at the back of the upper arm, the larger of the arm's two main muscles.
Exercises that mainly work your legs.Shoulder press: The shoulder press builds the deltoids, and overhead lifting recruits the core for stability.
Exercises that mainly work your legs.Lat pulldown: Lat pulldowns work the broad back muscles and mimic a pull-up using a cable machine.
Exercises that mainly work your legs.Chest fly: Chest flies stretch and squeeze the pectoral muscles, working the upper body only.
Exercises that mainly work your legs.Sit-up: Sit-ups train the abs and hip flexors, which is mostly the core, not the legs.
Exercises that mainly work your legs.Russian twist: The Russian twist works the obliques on the sides of the waist, and its name is a mystery.
Exercises that mainly work your legs.Shrug: Shrugs train the trapezius muscles on your upper back and neck, with no leg involvement.
Exercises that mainly work your legs.Skull crusher: A scary-sounding triceps exercise where you lower weights toward your forehead, hence the name.
Exercises that mainly work your legs.Arm circle: Arm circles warm up the shoulders, and they are a classic gym-class warm-up move.

Terrible places to take a nap.Volcano: Active volcanoes can have gases like carbon dioxide and sulfur dioxide seep out quietly, so even a calm-looking slope can be deadly.
Terrible places to take a nap.Shark tank: Many sharks must keep moving to push water over their gills, but plenty can rest on the sea floor, and none would pass up a snack.
Terrible places to take a nap.Ant hill: A colony can hold hundreds of thousands of ants, and fire ants swarm and sting together, which makes a nap on their mound a painful mistake.
Terrible places to take a nap.Beehive: A hive holds up to tens of thousands of bees that defend the queen, and a disturbed colony can chase an intruder surprisingly far.
Terrible places to take a nap.Lion's den: Lions sleep up to 20 hours a day, so any nap in their den would be an uninvited visit, and the Bible's Daniel is the famous survivor.
Terrible places to take a nap.Airport runway: Runways are built to handle aircraft touching down at roughly 250 km/h, and planes can land and take off every minute or two.
Terrible places to take a nap.Cactus patch: Cactus spines are modified leaves, and some, like cholla, detach so easily that people say they jump at you.
Terrible places to take a nap.Bowling lane: Lanes are coated with oil in carefully designed patterns, making them slippery, and a rolling ball weighs up to 7 kilograms.
Terrible places to take a nap.Busy highway: Cars at highway speed cover about 30 meters every second, so even a brief nap on the road leaves no time for anyone to react.
Terrible places to take a nap.Alligator pond: Alligators can stay nearly motionless for hours and burst into action in a flash, making a lakeside nap a risky one.
Terrible places to take a nap.Wasp nest: Wasps, unlike honeybees, can sting repeatedly, and a disturbed nest releases chemicals that call the rest of the colony to attack.
Terrible places to take a nap.Hammock: Hammocks were invented by people in Central and South America, and sailors adopted them since they stay level while a ship rocks.
Terrible places to take a nap.Bed: People have slept on raised beds for thousands of years, and the oldest known bedding, made of grass and leaves, is around 200,000 years old.
Terrible places to take a nap.Couch: Couch comes from the French coucher, to lie down. Naps on one are so common that doctors say a short snooze can boost alertness.
Terrible places to take a nap.Recliner: The first recliner was meant to be a chair for outdoor use; a 1928 Michigan company made it as a folding porch chair that people started using as bedroom furniture.
Terrible places to take a nap.Bunk bed: Bunk beds were used on ships and in military barracks to save space. A good nap spot, despite a risky top-bunk fall.
Terrible places to take a nap.Sleeping bag: Modern sleeping bags use down or synthetic fill, and early ones included a wool-lined style for explorers in cold climates.
Terrible places to take a nap.Futon: The futon is a Japanese bedding tradition, a folding cotton mattress rolled up in the morning, which is a very sensible nap spot.
Terrible places to take a nap.Air mattress: Air mattresses became popular for camping and guests; they slowly lose air as temperature drops overnight, but won't hurt you.
Terrible places to take a nap.Waterbed: The modern waterbed arrived in 1968, designed by a San Francisco design student, and it peaked in popularity in the 1980s.
Terrible places to take a nap.Cot: The word cot comes from Hindi, where khat means a bedstead. Folding cots were widely used in the army and by campers.
Terrible places to take a nap.Daybed: A daybed is made for daytime rest, so a nap there is its whole purpose, and it has been a seat and a bed since antiquity.
Terrible places to take a nap.Bean bag chair: The bean bag chair was invented in Italy in 1968 and called Sacco; it molds to the sleeper's shape, which makes napping easy.
Terrible places to take a nap.Four-poster bed: Four-poster beds had curtains in medieval times to keep out drafts and bugs, and the Great Bed of Ware held a dozen people.

You say \"a pair of\" these.Scissors: Scissors are always 'a pair of' because the two blades work together, and the word comes from Latin 'cisorium', meaning cutting tool.
You say \"a pair of\" these.Pants: Pants are 'a pair' because they began as two separate leg coverings, one for each leg, rather than one garment.
You say \"a pair of\" these.Glasses: Glasses are 'a pair' from the two lenses, and the earliest ones, from 13th-century Italy, were two lenses riveted together.
You say \"a pair of\" these.Socks: Socks come in two, and a sock's partner is famously the first thing to go missing in the laundry.
You say \"a pair of\" these.Shoes: Shoes come in two, and left and right shoes only became standard in the 1800s, since earlier ones were identical.
You say \"a pair of\" these.Gloves: Gloves come as a pair, and the term 'throw down the gauntlet' comes from knights tossing a glove as a challenge.
You say \"a pair of\" these.Earrings: Earrings come as a pair, and ear piercing is ancient, as the 5,000-year-old Otzi the Iceman had pierced ears.
You say \"a pair of\" these.Chopsticks: Chopsticks are a pair, and they've been used in China for over 3,000 years.
You say \"a pair of\" these.Binoculars: Binoculars are two linked telescopes, which is why we say 'a pair', and the two eyepieces give a 3D view.
You say \"a pair of\" these.Tongs: Tongs are a pair of arms joined at one end, and blacksmiths have used them since ancient times to hold hot metal.
You say \"a pair of\" these.Pliers: Pliers are a pair of pivoted handles with jaws, and the word comes from a French word meaning to bend or fold.
You say \"a pair of\" these.Jeans: Jeans are 'a pair' like pants, and they're named after the Genoese sailors' cloth, 'bleu de Genes'.
You say \"a pair of\" these.Tweezers: Tweezers are a pair of pinching arms, and the name comes from 'etui', an old word for a small case of instruments.
You say \"a pair of\" these.Hat: A trap: a hat is a single item, so you would never say 'a pair of hats', though you might say a pair of them in a list.
You say \"a pair of\" these.Scarf: A scarf is a single piece, so 'a pair of scarves' isn't how we say it, although it seems like it could work.
You say \"a pair of\" these.Watch: A watch is one object, and the first wristwatch was made for a Hungarian countess in 1868.
You say \"a pair of\" these.Necklace: A necklace is one chain around the neck, and the oldest known beads are about 100,000 years old.
You say \"a pair of\" these.Belt: A belt is a single band, and while we say 'a pair of pants', the belt that holds them up stands alone.
You say \"a pair of\" these.Necktie: A necktie is one piece, and it descends from the cravat, which French soldiers inherited from Croatian mercenaries.
You say \"a pair of\" these.Sweater: A sweater is a single garment, and the name came from a woolen garment athletes wore to sweat off weight.
You say \"a pair of\" these.Wallet: A wallet is one folded item, and the word comes from a Middle English word for a bag.
You say \"a pair of\" these.Umbrella: An umbrella is one object, and Chinese people made oiled-paper ones thousands of years ago, mostly to block the sun.
You say \"a pair of\" these.Backpack: A backpack is one bag, though it has two straps, which tempts people into saying a pair, but that's not how we say it.
You say \"a pair of\" these.Shirt: A shirt is a single garment, even though it has two sleeves, so we wouldn't say 'a pair of shirts' for one.

Awful to be stuck in an elevator with.Skunk: A skunk's spray can hit a target about three metres away and linger for days; in a elevator, there's no escape.
Awful to be stuck in an elevator with.Swarm of bees: A swarm of bees means hundreds of stinging, buzzing insects in a tiny closed box, with no room to flee.
Awful to be stuck in an elevator with.Bagpipe player: Bagpipes can hit about 100 decibels, as loud as a chainsaw, so a elevator's walls would bounce the sound everywhere.
Awful to be stuck in an elevator with.Durian: Durian is banned from many hotels and public transport in Southeast Asia; its smell is compared to rotten onions and gym socks.
Awful to be stuck in an elevator with.Wet dog: Wet dogs release a musty smell from the oils and microbes in their fur, and shaking spreads it all around.
Awful to be stuck in an elevator with.Goat: Male goats scent-mark themselves with urine, giving them a famously strong smell that fills a small space.
Awful to be stuck in an elevator with.Rooster: Roosters crow at about 100 decibels, loud enough to cause hearing damage at close range, and they don't just crow at dawn.
Awful to be stuck in an elevator with.Rattlesnake: Rattlesnakes warn with a rattle made of keratin segments that vibrate, and a trapped one is a dangerous neighbour.
Awful to be stuck in an elevator with.Smelly cheese: Strong cheeses like Limburger smell of feet because the same bacteria that cause foot odour help ripen them.
Awful to be stuck in an elevator with.Drummer: A drummer in a small box means a nonstop racket; and drums can reach well over 100 decibels.
Awful to be stuck in an elevator with.Porcupine: Porcupines can't shoot quills, but they have around 30,000 of them, and they stick easily on contact.
Awful to be stuck in an elevator with.Book: A trap: a book is a perfect companion. Most stalls end within an hour, but a good book makes any wait feel shorter.
Awful to be stuck in an elevator with.Snacks: Snacks would be welcome; elevator stalls rarely last long, but a bite helps when you're stuck with a skunk or a drummer.
Awful to be stuck in an elevator with.Phone charger: A phone charger helps keep your phone alive for calling help, which is the most valuable item you could have.
Awful to be stuck in an elevator with.Best friend: A best friend makes waiting bearable; shared stress and laughter make time feel shorter.
Awful to be stuck in an elevator with.Water bottle: Water bottles help, since people can go weeks without food but only days without water.
Awful to be stuck in an elevator with.Deck of cards: A deck of cards offers a huge number of games; there are more possible shuffles than atoms on Earth.
Awful to be stuck in an elevator with.Flashlight: A flashlight helps if the lights fail, though most elevators have emergency lighting, an alarm button and an intercom.
Awful to be stuck in an elevator with.Comedian: Comedians would be a welcome distraction when stuck; laughter reduces stress hormones in the body.
Awful to be stuck in an elevator with.Pillow: A pillow is handy if the wait is long, although elevator stalls are almost always fixed or rescued within the hour.
Awful to be stuck in an elevator with.Crossword: Crosswords are a fine way to pass time, and the first one was printed in a newspaper in 1913.
Awful to be stuck in an elevator with.Granola bar: A granola bar is pocket-sized energy; stuck in a stalled elevator, it's useful, calm company and no trouble to anyone.
Awful to be stuck in an elevator with.Board game: Board games are bulky to carry, but a stalled elevator with one becomes game night, which beats sharing space with a skunk.
Awful to be stuck in an elevator with.Handheld fan: A handheld fan helps in a stuffy cabin, and you won't run out of air; elevators aren't airtight, so ventilation continues.

Things a pirate would say.Arr: Arr is the classic pirate sound, popularised by actor Robert Newton in the 1950 film Treasure Island.
Things a pirate would say.Ahoy: Ahoy is an old sailors' greeting for hailing a ship, and Alexander Graham Bell wanted it for answering phones, before hello won.
Things a pirate would say.Shiver me timbers: Shiver me timbers is a pirate cry of surprise, about the ship's timbers shaking in storms; it appeared in Treasure Island.
Things a pirate would say.Walk the plank: Walking the plank is mostly a legend; documented cases of pirates making victims do so are very rare.
Things a pirate would say.Avast: Avast means stop or hold, from Dutch 'hou vast' meaning hold fast; sailors have used it for centuries.
Things a pirate would say.Yo ho ho: Yo ho ho is from the song in Treasure Island, 'Fifteen men on the dead man's chest', by Robert Louis Stevenson.
Things a pirate would say.Land ho: Land ho is a sailor's shout when land is first spotted from a ship, a true seafaring phrase.
Things a pirate would say.Matey: Matey is a friendly way for sailors to address a shipmate, from 'mate', a word used at sea since the 1400s.
Things a pirate would say.Pieces of eight: Pieces of eight were Spanish silver dollars, divided into eight reales, and they were the first global currency.
Things a pirate would say.Scallywag: Scallywag is a mischievous rogue; it likely originated from 1800s American slang and not from the pirate era.
Things a pirate would say.Thar she blows: Thar she blows is a whaler's cry, shouted when a whale's spout was spotted, not strictly a pirate phrase.
Things a pirate would say.Weigh anchor: Weigh anchor means to lift the anchor and set sail; it's not about weight but a form of old verb 'weigh' meaning lift.
Things a pirate would say.Yee-haw: Yee-haw is a cowboy cheer, from the American West, and never heard on the high seas.
Things a pirate would say.Howdy partner: Howdy partner is cowboy talk, a short form of 'How do you do', from the American frontier.
Things a pirate would say.Cowabunga: Cowabunga was popularised by the Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles, though it came from the 1950s TV show Howdy Doody.
Things a pirate would say.D'oh: D'oh is Homer Simpson's catchphrase, so common that it entered the Oxford English Dictionary in 2001.
Things a pirate would say.Ho ho ho: Ho ho ho is Santa Claus's laugh, and not a pirate's, despite sounding like 'yo ho ho'.
Things a pirate would say.Bazinga: Bazinga is Sheldon's catchphrase from The Big Bang Theory, and it means 'gotcha' after a joke.
Things a pirate would say.Abracadabra: Abracadabra is a magician's word, believed to be from Aramaic, and was once used in healing charms.
Things a pirate would say.Beam me up: Beam me up is from Star Trek, though the exact line 'Beam me up, Scotty' was never spoken in the original show.
Things a pirate would say.Hasta la vista: Hasta la vista is Spanish for 'until we see each other', and became famous from Terminator 2 in 1991.
Things a pirate would say.Exterminate: Exterminate is the Daleks' cry in Doctor Who, shouted in a robotic voice.
Things a pirate would say.Hakuna matata: Hakuna matata is Swahili for 'no worries', and it was made famous by The Lion King in 1994.
Things a pirate would say.Elementary: Elementary is Sherlock Holmes territory; the line 'Elementary, my dear Watson' never appears in Conan Doyle's stories.

Things a doctor uses.Stethoscope: Laennec's 1816 stethoscope was a paper tube, and he named it from the Greek for chest and I examine.
Things a doctor uses.Otoscope: An otoscope lights the ear canal and eardrum, and its name comes from the Greek word for ear.
Things a doctor uses.Tongue depressor: A tongue depressor is a flat wooden stick, and kids' craft projects now use millions of them.
Things a doctor uses.Syringe: The hypodermic syringe was developed in the 1850s, and it made precise injections possible.
Things a doctor uses.Scalpel: The scalpel's name comes from Latin for a small knife, and its blade is replaceable.
Things a doctor uses.Blood pressure cuff: A blood pressure cuff measures pressure in millimeters of mercury, and the first one was invented in the 1880s.
Things a doctor uses.Reflex hammer: A reflex hammer taps the knee, which tests a nerve loop that bypasses the brain.
Things a doctor uses.Thermometer: A thermometer measures fever, and normal body temperature averages close to 98.6 degrees Fahrenheit.
Things a doctor uses.Bandage: Bandages date to ancient Egypt, where linen strips wrapped wounds, and mummies.
Things a doctor uses.Whisk: A whisk whips air into eggs and cream, and it has no place in an exam room; the tool a doctor shares with the kitchen is the thermometer.
Things a doctor uses.Trowel: A trowel is a gardener's or bricklayer's tool, and the pointed mason's version spreads mortar for walls, not medicine.
Things a doctor uses.Gavel: A gavel is the judge's mallet, though in the US courts real judges rarely use one; it's far more common in meetings and on TV.
Things a doctor uses.Easel: An easel holds a painter's canvas upright, and the word comes from the Dutch ezel, meaning donkey, as it carries the load.
Things a doctor uses.Anvil: An anvil is a blacksmith's heavy iron block for shaping hot metal, and a big one can weigh hundreds of pounds.
Things a doctor uses.Plunger: A plunger belongs to the plumber, and the rubber-cup design was patented in 1874 by John Hawley.
Things a doctor uses.Chisel: A chisel is a carpenter's tool, though surgeons do use specialized osteotomes, a bone-cutting cousin of the chisel.
Things a doctor uses.Ladle: A ladle is a soup server, and it's been a kitchen basic since the Bronze Age.
Things a doctor uses.Spirit level: A spirit level has a trapped air bubble in liquid to show a flat surface, a tool for builders, not clinics.
Things a doctor uses.Rake: A rake gathers leaves and soil in the garden, and has nothing to do with healing.
Things a doctor uses.Megaphone: A megaphone amplifies a voice for a crowd, and the cheerleader's horn is as far from a quiet clinic as you get.
Things a doctor uses.Compass: A compass uses Earth's magnetic field to point north, so it's a navigator's tool, not a doctor's.
Things a doctor uses.Paintbrush: A paintbrush may use bristles from hog, sable or nylon, but a doctor's brush stays in the art studio, not the clinic.
Things a doctor uses.Hoe: A hoe is a long-handled gardening tool for weeding, among the oldest farm tools in the world.
Things a doctor uses.Abacus: An abacus is an ancient counting frame still used in parts of Asia, while modern doctors use calculators for dosages.

Things in a bank.Vault: Old bank vaults use time locks that cannot be opened even by the manager until a set hour, a design from the 1870s.
Things in a bank.Teller: The word teller comes from the old verb "tell," meaning to count, so a teller was literally the person counting money.
Things in a bank.ATM: The first cash machine appeared in London in 1967 and could only dispense a fixed amount of cash with a special voucher.
Things in a bank.Safe deposit box: Bank staff can't see inside your box, because it takes two keys, yours and the bank's, to open it.
Things in a bank.Loan officer: A loan officer's job is to judge how likely you are to repay, using your income, debts and credit history.
Things in a bank.Deposit slip: A deposit slip lists the cash and checks being paid in, and the paper is often still used even in the age of apps.
Things in a bank.Security camera: Banks are among the earliest users of surveillance cameras, and robbery films usually find them in the first scenes.
Things in a bank.Counting machine: Modern counters can sort and total notes at over a thousand a minute and spot counterfeits by magnetic ink.
Things in a bank.Teller window: Many teller windows have bullet-resistant glass, and have since the 1920s, when bank robberies were common.
Things in a bank.Night deposit box: A night drop lets businesses put in the day's takings after closing, and a chute carries it to a locked bag inside.
Things in a bank.Fire pole: A fire pole belongs to a fire station and a vault has no need for one.
Things in a bank.Dental chair: A dentist's chair is for teeth, and a bank only worries about cavities in the vault's security.
Things in a bank.Operating table: An operating table is for surgery, and while a mortgage can be painful, banks leave the surgery to hospitals.
Things in a bank.Pizza oven: An oven is for baking, and the only thing a bank bakes is interest.
Things in a bank.Hay bale: Hay is for farms, but oddly "farm" banks do exist, and they lend to growers rather than store hay.
Things in a bank.Jury box: A jury box is a courtroom feature, and while bank cases get tried there, it won't be found in a bank.
Things in a bank.Pulpit: A pulpit is a church fixture, though the old "Cathedral" style bank buildings were designed to inspire the same awe.
Things in a bank.Altar: Some grand old banks resemble temples, with columns and domes, but the altar remains a church thing.
Things in a bank.Bunk bed: Bunk beds are for sleeping, and the only thing "bunking" in a bank is the cash in the vault.
Things in a bank.Barber's chair: A barber chair would be at the barbershop, and a bank only cuts rates.
Things in a bank.Car lift: A car lift is for garages, though a drive-through bank lane does serve customers in their cars.
Things in a bank.Jukebox: Jukeboxes live in diners, and a bank's idea of music is quiet background tunes at best.
Things in a bank.Trampoline: Trampolines are for fun, and bank staff aim to keep deposits steady rather than bouncing.
Things in a bank.Bowling pins: Pins belong at a bowling alley, and a bank prefers to keep its balance rather than get a strike.

Fictional detectives.Encyclopedia Brown: Encyclopedia Brown is a boy detective from Donald Sobol's books, who solves cases with clues for readers to spot.
